1156.title: Silence is praise (Psalm 65:2)
1156.hook: we can say what God is not better than what God is; "for Thee silence is praise"
1156.howItsDone: In the Amidah, which is said quietly, those who pray it praise God as great, mighty and awesome, the words Rabbi Hanina defended. Students of the Guide study Maimonides' teaching on negative attributes in the chapters around 1:58–59.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Torah speaking in human language, words fitted to the listener. Your line: the torah speaks our language. Today, what happens when words run out.

A prayer leader stands before the congregation, and he's on a roll. The prayer has three words for God: great, mighty, awesome. He keeps going. Glorious, powerful, feared, strong, certain, honored. The list grows. In the room sits Rabbi Hanina, and he waits until the man is done. Then he asks him, quietly: have you finished all the praises of your Master? The Talmud keeps that question, and Maimonides picks it up in the Guide.
screen: `GREAT, MIGHTY, AWESOME.` → `AND MORE, AND MORE.` → `HAVE YOU FINISHED?`

segments.voice: Silence is praise. First, the rabbi's point. Rabbi Hanina goes on: even the three words we say, we would not dare to say if Moses had not used them in the Torah and the sages had not set them in the prayer. Then a parable. It's like a king who owns gold, and people praise him for owning silver. The praise isn't too much. It's too small, and it insults. Second, Maimonides' turn. In the Guide he argues that any positive word for God, even a grand one, borrows from our own world and falls short. What we can say more truly is what God is not. Not a body. Not limited. Not weak, not ignorant, not made of parts. Each no, he says, brings you a little nearer, the way ruling out what something isn't sharpens what you know. Third, the verse. In Hebrew, Psalm sixty-five begins its praise with the words l'kha dumiyah tehillah. Translations differ, and some English versions say praise waits for God. Maimonides reads it: for You, silence is praise. Not silence as having nothing to say. Silence as the right response once words run out. Fourth, the balance. He doesn't throw out prayer. The fixed words stay, because the Torah and the sages gave them. What he warns against is piling on more, as if more words were more honor. So the prayer is said, and then the silence after it says the rest.
screen: `GOLD PRAISED AS SILVER.` · `SAY WHAT GOD IS NOT.` · `FOR YOU, SILENCE IS PRAISE.` · `SAY THE WORDS, THEN STOP.` · then, large: `SILENCE IS PRAISE.`

segments.voice: If it fits your beliefs, say quietly one thing God is not, not a body, not small, and let each no stand by itself for a breath. If God isn't part of how you see things, take something vast, the sea or the night sky, and say what it isn't: not a pond, not a ceiling. Then stop adding words, and let the quiet be there.
Silence is praise. Maimonides' reading of Psalm sixty-five: since we can say more truly what God is not than what God is, silence becomes a form of praise. Today's word.
Your line: silence is praise. Some things are honored best by stopping. See you tomorrow.

1157.title: The hand is a metaphor
1157.hook: God's "hand" and "eye" are figures of speech
1157.howItsDone: Students of the Mishneh Torah read Maimonides' text together with the Raavad's printed glosses, weighing both. Some commentators on the Torah also explain bodily words for God as figures of speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Hanina's question, and saying what God is not. Your line: silence is praise. Today, one of the Torah's boldest pictures.

"For with a strong hand hath the LORD brought thee out of Egypt." That line is in the Torah, and it's written inside the tefillin some Jews bind on the arm and head. A strong hand. For some readers, an image comes with it: an enormous arm reaching down out of the clouds. Maimonides spent real effort trying to take that picture down. And a scholar who read him closely pushed back, not on the picture, but on how harshly to judge the people who kept it.
screen: `A STRONG HAND.` → `AN ARM FROM THE CLOUDS?` → `A PICTURE TO TAKE DOWN.`

segments.voice: The hand is a metaphor. First, the list. In the opening laws of the Mishneh Torah, Maimonides gathers the Torah's bodily words for God: under God's feet, written with God's finger, the hand of the LORD, the eyes of the LORD, the ears of the LORD. All of these, he says, are spoken according to what human minds can grasp. God has no body. Second, what each organ is doing. In the Guide he explains the pattern: an eye stands for perceiving, an ear for hearing, a hand for acting. When the Psalm says, "The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous," it means God's care reaches them. The strong hand that brought Israel out of Egypt means God's power at work. The picture points at an action, not a limb. Third, the stakes. In his Laws of Repentance, Maimonides lists someone who says God has a body or form among those who deny a core belief. Fourth, the pushback. Rabbi Abraham ben David, known as the Raavad, wrote short critical notes on the code. On this line he wrote, in effect: why call such a person that? People greater and better than he followed this idea, because of what they read in the verses and in the midrash. The Raavad wasn't saying God has a body. He was defending the sincere reader who took the words plainly. Printed editions carry his notes beside the code: the code, and a reader who argued with it, side by side.

Notice whether it feels farther away, or closer.
The hand is a metaphor. Maimonides' teaching that God's hand, eyes and ears in scripture are figures for God's acting, caring and hearing, since God has no body. Today's word.

1158.title: Prophecy needs preparation
1158.hook: prophecy requires mind, character and imagination
1158.howItsDone: Jews who study Maimonides read his account of prophecy in the Laws of the Foundations of the Torah, chapter seven, and in the second part of the Guide. Tradition holds that prophecy has ceased, so the teaching is studied as a picture of human readiness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the strong hand as a picture of God's power, and the Raavad defending the plain reader. Your line: the hand is a metaphor. Today, a prophet who asks for music.

Three kings and their armies are stuck in a desert with no water, and they come to the prophet Elisha for a word from God. He has hard words for one of them, the king of Israel. Then he asks for something odd. Not a scroll, not an altar. A musician. "But now bring me a minstrel." The musician plays, and the text says the hand of the LORD came upon him, and he speaks. Why would a prophet need music first? Maimonides has an answer.
screen: `NO WATER IN THE DESERT.` → `ELISHA'S HARD WORDS.` → `BRING ME A MINSTREL.`

segments.voice: Prophecy needs preparation. First, the mind. In his law code, Maimonides writes that prophecy rests only on a person great in wisdom, strong in character, whose impulses never overpower them. The Guide explains why: prophecy flows from God first into a person's reasoning mind, and a mind that hasn't been trained has nowhere to hold it. Second, character. A person ruled by appetite, by greed, by the hunger for honor, is pulled too many ways to receive anything. So the work on character from his Eight Chapters, the middle way, isn't a separate subject. It's part of the same preparation. Third, imagination, the surprising one. Prophecy then flows into the imagination, he says, which is why prophets see visions, parables and dreams, not lectures. A philosopher with a strong mind but a weak imagination might understand deeply and still not be a prophet. And imagination is fragile: sadness and anger shut it down. That's how he reads Elisha: angered, he needed the music to bring back joy and calm before prophecy could come. Fourth, the limit. Does all this preparation guarantee prophecy? No. Even a fully prepared person may not receive it, Maimonides holds, if God withholds it. Preparation doesn't force the gift. It makes a person able to hold it. For him, that's the line between a vessel and a demand.
screen: `A TRAINED MIND.` · `A STEADY CHARACTER.` · `A LIVELY IMAGINATION.` · `READY IS NOT GUARANTEED.` · then, large: `PREPARE THE VESSEL.`

segments.voice: Check in on the three things Maimonides names: is your mind rested or scattered, is your character pulled by irritation, wanting or worry, is there room in you for a picture or a song? Pick the one that needs the most care, and let one small kindness toward it come to mind: a page of real reading, a grudge set down, or a piece of music, the way Elisha asked.

1159.title: Reasons for the commandments
1159.hook: Maimonides looks for reasons behind the laws; others say some have none we can know
1159.howItsDone: Jewish study of a commandment often asks both what the law requires and what its purpose might be. Some teachers draw on Maimonides' reasons; others, following Rashi on the red heifer, stress keeping the statutes as decrees.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prophecy's preparation: mind, character, imagination, and Elisha's minstrel. Your line: prepare the vessel. Today, a simple question about rules.

What is this for? Put that question to the commandments, and you meet two very different answers inside Judaism. One says: ask. There is wisdom here, and you can find it. The other says: some of these you keep because God commanded them, and the reason may stay hidden. Both answers come from teachers of the same Torah. Maimonides plants himself firmly on one side.
screen: `WHAT IS THIS FOR?` → `ASK, AND FIND WISDOM.` → `OR KEEP IT, REASON HIDDEN.`

segments.voice: Ta'amei hamitzvot: the reasons for the commandments. Ta'am is the word for taste, and also for reason, the flavor of sense inside a law. First, Maimonides' claim. In the third part of the Guide he says every commandment has a reason and serves a purpose: to teach a true idea, to correct a habit, to build a fair society. Some people dislike giving reasons, he notices, as if a law with no explanation were more divine. He thinks they have it backward, and quotes Deuteronomy, where the nations hear these laws and say, "Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people." How could they say that, he asks, if the laws made no sense? Second, his limit. The general purpose of each commandment has a reason, but not every detail. Why a lamb in one offering and a ram in another? Some choice had to be made, he says, and searching for a reason there is chasing nothing. Third, the other side. The Torah calls the red heifer ritual "the statute of the law," using the word chok, statute. Rashi explains it as a decree: God has decreed it, and a person has no right to question it. In the Talmud, the rabbis even suggest the reasons were left unrevealed for a purpose, warning that King Solomon, who thought he knew the reasons for the king's laws, stumbled. Fourth, what both sides share. Neither says to keep only the laws you understand. For Maimonides, the search for reasons deepens the keeping. For the other view, keeping without knowing is its own kind of trust.
screen: `EVERY COMMANDMENT HAS A PURPOSE.` · `REASONS FOR THE WHOLE, NOT EACH DETAIL.` · `A STATUTE: KEPT AS A DECREE.` · `BOTH KEEP THE LAW.` · then, large: `LOOKING FOR REASONS.`

segments.voice: Choose one practice you know, from Judaism or your own life, lighting candles, resting one day a week, no phones at dinner, and ask Maimonides' question: what is this for, what idea does it teach, what habit does it shape? Then ask the other question: is there something here I keep even without a full answer? Let both answers be there.

Your line: looking for reasons. A rule can be kept with a why, or kept in trust. That's one thousand one hundred fifty-nine days.

1160.title: Providence follows attention
1160.hook: he teaches that providence follows how closely the mind is joined to God
1160.howItsDone: Jewish teaching values kavanah, focused intention, in prayer and in keeping the commandments. Students of the Guide study Maimonides' view of providence in its third part, often alongside Hasidic teachings that God's care reaches every detail.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the reasons for the commandments: Maimonides searching for purpose, others keeping in trust. Your line: looking for reasons. Today, a leaf.

A leaf lets go of a branch and drifts down. A spider in the corner of a window catches a fly. Did God decide that this leaf would fall at this moment, and that this fly would be the one? Maimonides raises exactly these examples in the Guide, and his answer is blunt. No, he says. Not for the leaf, not for the fly. Then he turns to human beings, and his answer changes, but with a condition attached.
screen: `A LEAF FALLS.` → `A SPIDER CATCHES A FLY.` → `WAS THAT DECIDED?`

segments.voice: Providence follows attention. Providence means God's care and guidance over what happens. First, the leaf. In the third part of the Guide, Maimonides says that for plants and animals, God's providence watches over the species, not each individual. The falling leaf and the caught fly happen by the ordinary workings of nature. Second, the person. With human beings it's different. Providence over a person follows the divine overflow that reaches them, and that depends on their mind: the more a person's intellect is joined to God, the closer the care. It isn't handed out equally, like rain. Third, the palace. Near the end of the Guide, he tells a parable of a king in his palace and people at different distances from him, some still outside the walls, some in the inner rooms. And he adds a sharp point: when a person's mind is fully elsewhere, busy with other things, in that hour the bond is loosened. He reads the Psalm this way: "Because he hath set his love upon Me, therefore will I deliver him." Fourth, the other voices. This was a bold view, and not everyone held it. Later teachers, among them Hasidic masters, taught that God's care reaches every detail, and tradition says the Baal Shem Tov held that even a leaf turns in the wind by providence. Both views are still taught. Maimonides' version makes care something a person can move toward: turn the mind toward God, and keep it turned.

segments.voice: Give one thing your full attention: your breath, a single sound in the room, or, if you pray, one line of a prayer you know. When your mind wanders off to the day, notice it, the way Maimonides noticed the mind leaving the palace, and come back with no scolding. Each return is the practice.
Providence follows attention. Maimonides' teaching that God's care over a person grows with how closely their mind is turned to God, and loosens when the mind turns away. Today's word.
Your line: providence follows attention. For Maimonides, where the mind turns, care follows. See you tomorrow.

1161.title: Most harm we do ourselves
1161.hook: he argues most suffering comes from what people do to themselves and each other
1161.howItsDone: Jewish teaching on repentance asks a person to examine their own part in what went wrong, and some study Maimonides' account of the three kinds of evil in Guide 3:12 alongside his Laws of Repentance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the leaf, the palace, and care that follows the mind. Your line: providence follows attention. Today, suffering, sorted.

A writer once argued that the world holds more evil than good. Count up the pain, the sickness, the grief, he said, and the scale tips the wrong way. Maimonides answered it in the Guide. He didn't deny that suffering is real. He did something more uncomfortable. He sorted it, kind by kind, and asked where it actually comes from. And when the sorting was done, the biggest pile wasn't the one blamed on God or on nature.
screen: `MORE EVIL THAN GOOD?` → `SORT THE SUFFERING.` → `WHICH PILE IS BIGGEST?`

segments.voice: Most harm we do ourselves. From the Guide, part three, chapter twelve. First, the harm of having a body. Bodies come into being and wear out: illness, injury, the blows of nature. Real, Maimonides says, but the least frequent. Second, the harm people do to each other: tyranny, violence, war. More common than the first, but still not the largest. Third, the harm people do to themselves. This, he says, is the most frequent of all. Too much eating, too much drinking, appetites without limits, chasing more than anyone needs. A person wrecks their health, their peace, their relationships, and then complains about the world. Some readers find in his discussion that the hunger for luxuries also turns people against each other, so the third kind feeds the second. He quotes Ecclesiastes: "God made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions." Fourth, why the writer got it wrong. A person who thinks the whole universe exists for them judges everything by their own small hurts, and so concludes the world is mostly bad. Step back, and much of what we suffer turns out to be within reach of human choice. This is not a teaching that blames people for their illnesses or their grief. Maimonides keeps the first kind on the list. It hands back some power: the largest pile is one people can begin to shrink.
screen: `THE BODY WEARS OUT.` · `WHAT PEOPLE DO TO EACH OTHER.` · `WHAT PEOPLE DO TO THEMSELVES.` · `THE WORLD IS NOT ABOUT ME.` · then, large: `MOST HARM WE DO OURSELVES.`

segments.voice: Think back over the past week to one thing that went wrong, and sort it gently, the way Maimonides would: the body or nature simply happening, something another person did, or some small part that was yours, a habit, an excess, a word. Don't punish yourself; just find the part that's yours, and one step that would care for it. If what hurts ever feels like too much to carry, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

1162.hook: the Guide ends: know God, then practice kindness, justice and righteousness
1162.howItsDone: Jewish teaching often links knowing God with walking in God's ways, and some communities study the Guide's last chapter alongside acts of kindness, justice and charity in daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maimonides sorted suffering into three kinds and found the harm people bring on themselves the most frequent. Your line: most harm we do. Today, the last page of his Guide.

The final chapter of a long, difficult book. Maimonides has spent the whole Guide for the Perplexed on hard questions: what words about God can mean, how prophecy works, why the commandments exist. A reader might expect one last proof, sealed and abstract. Instead he sorts out what people chase in life, opens the book of Jeremiah, and lands on three plain Hebrew words: kindness, justice, righteousness. A whole philosophy ends at the door of an ordinary deed.
screen: `THE GUIDE'S LAST CHAPTER.` → `ONE LAST PROOF?` → `KINDNESS, JUSTICE, RIGHTEOUSNESS.`

segments.voice: Imitate God. First, four things people call perfection. Maimonides lists them in order: what you own, the health and strength of your body, good character, and true knowledge of God. Possessions can be gone overnight, he says, and were never really part of you. A strong body is something an animal has too. Good character is precious, but it mostly matters in how you deal with other people. Knowledge of God is the one that is truly your own. Second, Jeremiah seems to agree: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom," nor the mighty in his might, nor the rich in his riches. Glory instead in understanding and knowing God. So far the mind sounds like the finish line. Third, the verse keeps going. Jeremiah says what kind of God: the LORD who does mercy, justice and righteousness in the earth, "for in these things I delight, saith the LORD." In Hebrew, chesed, mishpat, tzedakah. Maimonides slows down here. The goal, he says, is to know God's ways, and whoever comes to know them will set out to act the same way. Fourth, this is a commandment, not only an ideal. In his law code he counts it from Deuteronomy, "and walk in His ways," with the rabbis' explanation: as God is called gracious, be gracious; as God is called merciful, be merciful. So a book written for a perplexed student ends with a person getting up to do one kind thing.
screen: `FOUR KINDS OF PERFECTION.` · `NOT WISDOM, MIGHT OR RICHES.` · `MERCY, JUSTICE, RIGHTEOUSNESS.` · `WALK IN HIS WAYS.` · then, large: `FOR IN THESE THINGS I DELIGHT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you'll see in the next day, and find one who could use something small: a ride, a message, a meal, a fair hearing, an apology you owe. Don't pick the grandest thing; pick the one you would actually do, and see yourself doing it, start to finish. If you pray, you can hold the words "and walk in His ways" for a few breaths.
